plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000064) on the WPA Pack Horse Library Project in eastern Kentucky (1935-1943): riders, routes, donated and mended materials, scrapbooks, readers. Topic checked against every bank and the combined bank (no matches). Ten new items weighted toward hard conventions (whom, dangling modifier, relevance) with two NO CHANGE keys. Plus E063-04 (NO CHANGE moved to A) and E063-06 (hint reworded) resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-E-000063. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Books on Horseback
passages.text:
[1] During the Great Depression, many families in the mountains of eastern Kentucky lived far from any library, and the roads that reached them were often little more than rocky creek beds. [2] In 1935, the Works Progress Administration (WPA), a federal agency that created jobs for the unemployed, began a program that brought books to these families in the only way {{1|possible; on horseback}}.

[3] The riders, most of {{2|them were women,}} were known as packhorse librarians. [4] Each rider followed a route that could cover many miles each week, carrying books and magazines in saddlebags to homes, one-room schools, and remote {{3|communities. Where}} no car could go. [5] {{4|Riding through rain and snow, the mountain trails were dangerous for the librarians.}} [6] When a trail grew too steep or muddy, the riders often {{5|have had to}} dismount and lead their horses or mules on foot.

[7] The books themselves posed a challenge. [8] The program had almost no money for buying materials, so nearly everything the librarians carried was donated, and much of it arrived worn or damaged. [9] {{6|However,}} the librarians did not throw these materials away. [10] They mended torn pages and pasted recipes, quilt patterns, and stories clipped from old magazines into handmade scrapbooks. {{7|}}

[11] For many families, a rider's visit was {{8|anticipated with eagerness and looked forward to}}. [12] Some readers asked for books about farming or health, and adults who had never learned to read sometimes asked their children {{9|to read aloud}} to them. [13] The program ended in 1943, when wartime jobs became plentiful and the WPA was shut down. [14] By then, the packhorse librarians had carried books to thousands of families who might otherwise have had almost none.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: began a program that brought books to these families
candidates.explanation: A colon after the complete clause correctly introduces the phrase that explains "the only way possible."

A.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "on horseback" is only a phrase.

B.rationale: A colon cannot separate a preposition from its object.

D.rationale: The comma after "on" splits the phrase "on horseback."

candidates.remember: A semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Most of whom were women" is a relative clause describing the riders; "whom" is the object of "of."

A.rationale: "Most of them were women" is an independent clause and cannot interrupt the sentence this way.

C.rationale: After the preposition "of," the object form "whom" is needed.

D.rationale: "Most of they" uses the subject pronoun after a preposition and leaves a clause wedged into the sentence.

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without the interrupting clause.

candidates.remember: Use "whom" as the object of a preposition.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: carrying books and magazines in saddlebags
candidates.explanation: "Where no car could go" describes the communities, so it belongs in the same sentence with no punctuation.

A.rationale: "Where no car could go" cannot stand alone as a sentence.

B.rationale: A semicolon cannot introduce a dependent clause.

C.rationale: A colon here wrongly separates the clause from the noun it describes.

hints: Can "Where no car could go" stand alone?

strategy.explanation: Test the part after the period on its own.

candidates.remember: A dependent clause cannot be its own sentence.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Riding through rain and snow, the librarians faced dangerous mountain trails.
choices.C: Riding through rain and snow, danger came to the librarians on the trails.
choices.D: Riding through rain and snow, the librarians' mountain trails were dangerous.

candidates.evidence: When a trail grew too steep or muddy
candidates.explanation: The phrase "Riding through rain and snow" must be followed by the people riding, the librarians.

A.rationale: The trails are not the ones riding, so the opening phrase dangles.

C.rationale: The danger is not doing the riding, so the modifier still dangles.

D.rationale: The subject is "trails," not the librarians, so the modifier still dangles.

strategy.explanation: Find the noun right after the comma.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier describes the noun right after it.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The essay describes past events, so the simple past "had to" is consistent.

A.rationale: The present perfect does not fit a narrative set in the 1930s.

B.rationale: The singular present perfect neither agrees with "riders" nor fits the past.

D.rationale: "Having" leaves the clause without a main verb.

strategy.explanation: Match the verb to the essay's time frame.

candidates.remember: Keep verb tense consistent with the narrative.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: much of it arrived worn or damaged
candidates.explanation: One might expect worn materials to be discarded, but the librarians kept them, so the contrast transition "However" fits.

B.rationale: Damaged materials are not a reason to keep them.

C.rationale: The sentence is not an example of materials arriving damaged.

D.rationale: The sentence does not describe something similar to the previous one.

hints: Is the sentence expected or unexpected given the last one?

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Quilting has a long history in Appalachia, where quilts were often made from scraps of worn-out clothing.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why the families valued the librarians' scrapbooks so highly.
choices.B: Yes, because it shows that the librarians made quilts as well as scrapbooks.
choices.C: No, because it contradicts the claim that the quilt patterns came from old magazines.
choices.D: No, because it shifts the focus from the librarians' work to the history of quilting.

candidates.evidence: pasted recipes, quilt patterns, and stories
candidates.explanation: The paragraph is about how the librarians reused donated materials; the history of quilting is a digression from that focus.

A.rationale: The sentence is about quilting in general; it does not mention the scrapbooks or why anyone valued them.

B.rationale: The sentence does not say the librarians made quilts.

C.rationale: The sentence is about how quilts were made, not about where the patterns came from, so it does not contradict anything.

strategy.explanation: Compare the sentence with the paragraph's focus.

candidates.remember: Leave out a sentence that strays from the paragraph's point.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: For many families, a rider's visit
candidates.explanation: "Eagerly awaited" says the idea once and clearly.

A.rationale: "Anticipated with eagerness" and "looked forward to" say the same thing.

hints: Which choice says the idea once?
candidates.remember: Avoid saying the same thing twice.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: adults who had never learned to read
candidates.explanation: "Ask" someone "to" do something, so "to read aloud" is idiomatic.

B.rationale: "Asked their children reading aloud" is not idiomatic.

C.rationale: "Asked their children for reading aloud" is not idiomatic.

D.rationale: "Asked their children with reading aloud" is not idiomatic.

strategy.explanation: Read each option in the sentence.

candidates.remember: "Ask" takes an infinitive: "ask someone to do."

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to describe how a government program helped people in one region gain access to reading material. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it focuses on how the WPA created jobs for unemployed people across the country.
choices.B: No, because it focuses mainly on the dangers of riding mountain trails in bad weather.
choices.C: Yes, because it explains how WPA riders brought reading material to families in eastern Kentucky.
choices.D: No, because it never identifies which agency ran the program or the year in which the program began.

candidates.evidence: began a program that brought books to these families
candidates.explanation: The essay describes a WPA program that delivered reading material to families in eastern Kentucky, which matches the purpose.

A.rationale: The essay mentions the WPA's purpose only briefly and focuses on one program in one region.

B.rationale: The weather is one detail; most of the essay is about delivering and reusing reading material.

D.rationale: Sentence 2 names the WPA and the year 1935.

hints: What is the whole essay about?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against the exact purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: also tucked roads below for crosstown traffic
choices.C: tucked also roads for crosstown traffic
choices.D: also tucked, for crosstown traffic, roads

candidates.evidence: below the level of the park
candidates.explanation: "Also tucked roads for crosstown traffic below the level of the park" keeps each modifier next to the words it modifies.

B.rationale: "Below" is now separated from "the level of the park" and the sentence becomes confusing.

C.rationale: Placing "also" between the verb and its object is awkward and unidiomatic.

D.rationale: Setting off "for crosstown traffic" separates the verb from its object awkwardly.

strategy.explanation: Read each option in the full sentence.

candidates.remember: Keep modifiers next to the words they describe.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: a community of mostly African American
candidates.explanation: The community was made up of many homeowners, so the plural "homeowners" with no apostrophe is correct.

A.rationale: "Homeowner's" is singular possessive, but the sentence needs a plural noun.

B.rationale: "Homeowners'" is a plural possessive, but nothing follows that they possess.

C.rationale: "Homeowner" is singular, but a community has many homeowners.

hints: Is the word plural, possessive, or both?
